sit: You are the first forward entering the offensive zone with the puck. The defenseman is backing up quickly. What should you scan for first?
opts: The exact distance between your stick and the puck
The space between you and the backing up defenseman to see if you have room to skate
Your own defensemen trailing far behind the play
The goalie's feet to see if they are in the butterfly
explain: Reading the gap of the defender tells you if you can drive the puck wide, or if you need to delay and look for a teammate. If they back up fast, you have space to use.

sit: When skating back to retrieve a puck in your defensive corner, you should wait until you have the puck on your stick before looking around.
tip: Do your work before the puck arrives.
why: Looking over your shoulder before you touch the puck helps you spot the forechecker and find your open teammate early.

sit: A winger is waiting on the boards for a breakout pass. They stare directly at the puck the entire time it slides toward them, catch it, and immediately get checked.
question: What is the player's mistake?
opts: They did not skate toward the center of the ice before catching it
They failed to shoulder check into the middle of the ice to see the incoming pressure
They should have batted the puck out of the air instead of waiting for it to slide
They caught the pass on their forehand instead of their backhand
explain: Hockey Canada teaches wingers to shoulder check the middle of the ice before the puck arrives so they know if they have time to turn or if they need to protect it immediately.

sit: You are the center supporting your defenseman low in the zone. You see your winger is open on the far boards, but a forechecker is skating hard at you.
opts: Turn your back to the play and try to stickhandle through the forechecker
One-touch pass the puck quickly to the open winger on the far boards before the pressure hits
Hold the puck and skate straight backward into your own goalie
Flip the puck as high as you can directly into the ceiling
explain: Because you already scanned and saw the open winger, you can make a quick, safe play to the open space away from the pressure.
tip: Let the puck do the work by passing away from the pressure.

sit: You are playing defense and catch a pass at the offensive blue line. Before you decide to shoot, what is the most important thing to scan the scoring area for?
opts: Whether the other team's coach is watching you
If there is a clear lane to the net and if you have a teammate screening the goalie
If the puck is perfectly flat on the ice with no snow on it
Whether your other defenseman is ready for a drop pass
explain: USA Hockey ADM stresses that point shots are most effective when there is traffic and a clear lane. Shooting into shin pads causes breakaways.

sit: You are the first player back for a puck retrieval. Put these actions in the correct order to make a smart play.
items: Take a quick shoulder check to locate the forechecker
Pick up the puck on your stick
Use your skating edges to create separation from the pressure
Make a crisp pass to your supporting teammate
explain: Scanning always happens first. Once you know where the pressure is, you can collect the puck, create space, and execute the pass.

sit: You are away from the puck in the offensive zone while your teammate is battling in the corner. How should you use your eyes?
opts: Watch the puck battle closely so you know exactly who wins it
Keep your head on a swivel to find an open pocket of space away from defenders
Stare down the opposing goalie to try and distract them
Look at your own bench to see if it is time to change
explain: Scanning away from the puck allows you to find soft spots in the coverage. If your teammate wins the puck, you are already in a great position to receive a pass.

sit: You are regrouping in the neutral zone. You look up and see the opposing defensemen are standing completely still at their blue line. What is your next move?
opts: Dump the puck gently into their skates
Pass the puck backward to slow the game down
Attack the space with speed to force them to pivot or back up
Stop skating and wait for them to make the first move
explain: Flat-footed defenders are vulnerable to speed. Scanning their feet tells you that you have the advantage if you attack quickly.

sit: You are bringing the puck up the ice on a rush. You see the first layer of defense stepping up on you. Why is it critical to scan the second layer behind them?
opts: To know if you can chip the puck into space and retrieve it behind the first defender
So you can aim a slapshot directly at the second defender
To make sure the referee is keeping up with the play
Because the second defender is always the one who will check you
explain: Scanning beyond the immediate pressure helps you identify open space. If there is a gap between the first and second layers, a chip-and-chase or area pass is highly effective.

sit: When playing weak-side wing in the defensive zone, it is best to stay locked onto the puck so you never lose track of the play.
tip: Keep your head on a swivel.
why: Staring only at the puck causes you to lose your check. You must constantly scan between the puck and the high forward creeping into the slot.

sit: A defenseman receives a D-to-D pass in the neutral zone. They look down to catch it cleanly, hold onto it for three seconds while looking for a pass, and get hit by the forechecker.
question: What is the player's mistake?
opts: They did not shoot the puck into the offensive zone immediately
They failed to scan up the ice before the pass arrived, resulting in slow decision making
They caught the pass on their backhand
They should have skated directly at the forechecker to draw a penalty
explain: Pre-scanning allows players to map the ice. Without taking a picture before the puck arrives, you waste valuable time trying to process the play while holding the puck.

sit: Your team is cycling the puck low in the offensive zone. You are the high forward (F3). You scan the slot and see it is completely empty.
opts: Retreat back to the center red line to play defense
Dive into the empty slot and present your stick for a quick scoring chance
Skate down into the corner to make it a 3-on-2 battle
Stand exactly where you are and wait for a rebound
explain: Scanning away from the puck reveals soft spots in the defense. Finding that quiet ice in the slot makes you a dangerous passing option for the cycle.
tip: Find the quiet ice and show your target.

sit: You are a winger slashing across the neutral zone to receive a breakout pass. Order the steps for a successful entry.
items: Scan the offensive blue line to locate the defensemen's gap
Present a clear target with your stick to your passing defenseman
Catch the puck in stride while maintaining your speed
Read the gap to decide whether to carry, chip, or pass
explain: You must scan the opposing defense before calling for the puck. Once you catch it, your previous scan allows you to make an instant, informed read on the entry.

sit: You are a defenseman defending a 2-on-1 rush. What should your eyes be doing as the play crosses your blue line?
opts: Staring purely at the puck carrier's chest to prepare for a body check
Looking back at your own goalie to see if they are ready
Quickly shifting focus back and forth between the puck carrier and the dangerous pass option
Watching the puck carrier's skates to see what edge they are on
explain: On an odd-man rush, you must scan actively to manage both threats. Monitoring the non-puck carrier ensures you can take away the dangerous backdoor pass.

sit: You pick up a loose puck in the high slot of your defensive zone. You feel pressure right on your back, but you haven't scanned up the ice yet.
opts: Throw a blind backhand pass toward the middle of the neutral zone
Protect the puck with your body and skate toward the safer boards to buy time to look up
Try a spin-o-rama move to shake the defender in the slot
Shoot the puck as hard as you can at the glass
explain: If you haven't scanned and have pressure in a dangerous area, protecting the puck and moving to safer ice (the boards) buys you the fraction of a second you need to get your eyes up.

sit: A good habit for a center on a faceoff win in the offensive zone is to immediately look at their own defenseman to ensure they caught the puck.
tip: Trust your teammates and find your assignment.
why: Once the puck goes back, the center must immediately scan the opposing forwards to block their path and start driving toward the net for a screen or tip.
